source: Round 5 HVAC/mechanical deepening (hvac5): IFGC 2021 Ch. 3-6, IMC 2021 Ch. 3-6 and 9, EPA 40 CFR 82 Subpart F and 40 CFR 84, DOE efficiency rules, and HVAC fundamentals

facts.fact: Under the 2021 IFGC, gas piping must be sized by one of three methods: the pipe sizing tables or equations in Section 402.4, the sizing tables in a listed piping system's installation instructions (for example, CSST), or engineering methods.
facts.note: Confirmed in Seattle's published 2021 Fuel Gas Code (2021 IFGC text; Washington does not amend IFGC 402).

facts.fact: Under IFGC 2021 402.2, the gas flow used to size piping is the sum of the maximum input ratings of all appliances served, assuming they all run at full capacity at once. A smaller (diversified) load may be used only where load diversity can be established.

IFGC 2021 Table 402.4(2) (Schedule 40 steel, natural gas, under 2 psi inlet, 0.5 in. w.c. drop, 0.60 specific gravity) lists these capacities in cubic feet per hour: at 10 ft, 1/2 in = 172, 3/4 in = 360, 1 in = 678, 1-1/4 in = 1,390; at 50 ft, 72, 151, 284 and 583; at 100 ft, 50, 104, 195 and 400.
facts.note: Values read from the 2021 IFGC table as published in Seattle's 2021 Fuel Gas Code.

facts.fact: Longest length method example (IFGC 2021 Table 402.4(2)): the run from the meter to the most remote appliance is 60 ft, so every section is sized from the 60 ft row. The main carrying 205 CFH needs 1 in pipe (257 CFH; 3/4 in holds only 137), a 100 CFH furnace branch needs 3/4 in (137), and a 40 CFH water heater branch needs 1/2 in (65).
facts.note: Worked example built from the published 60 ft row: 1/2 in 65, 3/4 in 137, 1 in 257, 1-1/4 in 528 CFH.

facts.fact: Under the 2021 IFGC, before adding an appliance to an existing gas system you must check that the piping has enough capacity, and enlarge it or run separate piping if it does not (401.4). Where separate customers on one premises have separate meters, their outlet piping may not be interconnected (401.6), and piping from multiple meters must be permanently marked to show which meter supplies it (401.7).

IFGC 2021 308.2 allows clearances to combustible material to be reduced only by a protection method in Table 308.2 or a listed clearance-reduction assembly (UL 1618). Clearances not shown in the table may be found by interpolation, but extrapolation below the table range is not allowed.

Per IFGC 2021 Table 308.2, No. 24 gage sheet metal spaced out 1 inch with a ventilated air space reduces a required 36 in clearance to 18 in above the appliance and 12 in at the sides and rear, and reduces a required 18 in clearance to 9 in above and 6 in at the sides and rear.

Per IFGC 2021 Table 308.2, a 3-1/2 inch masonry wall can reduce clearances only at the sides and rear (not above): without an air space, 36 in becomes 24 in and 18 in becomes 12 in; with a 1 inch ventilated air space, 36 in becomes 12 in and 18 in becomes 6 in.

Table 308.2 rules (IFGC 2021): spacers and ties must be noncombustible and may not be placed directly behind the appliance or connector; there must be at least 1 inch between the appliance and the protector; and mineral wool used in a protection system must have a density of at least 8 lb per cubic foot and a melting point of at least 1,500 F.

Under IFGC 2021 303.7, an appliance installed in a pit may not touch the soil; the pit sides must be held back at least 12 inches from the appliance (30 inches on the control side); pits more than 12 inches deep below grade need concrete or masonry walls extending at least 4 inches above grade; and the pit must be protected from flooding.

Under the 2021 IFGC, furnaces and boilers installed in closets or alcoves must be listed for that installation (303.5). Required clearances to combustibles must account for door swing, drawer pulls, overhead projections and shelving, and door stops or door closers may not be used to provide the clearance (305.8).

Under the 2021 IFGC, gas piping may never be used as a grounding electrode (309.1). Above-ground gas piping other than CSST that is likely to become energized must be electrically continuous and bonded; it is considered bonded when it is connected to an appliance that is connected to the equipment grounding conductor of its circuit (310.1).

In the 2021 IFGC, CSST that is not arc-resistant must be bonded to the electrical service grounding electrode system (or lightning protection system) with a jumper of at least 6 AWG copper, no longer than 75 ft, using UL 467 listed clamps (310.2). Arc-resistant CSST (ARCSST) only has to be electrically continuous and bonded to an effective ground-fault current path like other gas piping (310.3).
facts.note: The 2018 IFGC numbered the CSST bonding rule 310.1.1; the 2021 edition split it into 310.2 (standard CSST) and 310.3 (arc-resistant CSST).

facts.fact: Under IFGC 2021 307.5, a Category IV condensing appliance needs an auxiliary drain pan where damage to building components could result from a stopped condensate drain, unless the appliance automatically shuts down when its condensate drain is blocked.

IFGC 2021 501.8 lists appliances that do not need to be vented, including ranges, built-in domestic cooking units listed for optional venting, hot plates and laundry stoves, Type 1 clothes dryers (which are exhausted per Section 614), refrigerators, counter appliances, room heaters listed for unvented use, direct-fired makeup air heaters, and small specialty appliances such as laboratory burners and gas lights.

Under the 2021 IFGC, where unvented appliances (other than ranges, cooking units, hot plates and Type 1 dryers) total more than 20 Btu/h per cubic foot of room volume, enough of them must be vented to bring the unvented total down to 20 Btu/h per cubic foot. Example: a 2,000 cubic foot room may have at most 2,000 x 20 = 40,000 Btu/h of such unvented appliances.
facts.note: An adjoining room connected by an opening that cannot be closed may be counted in the volume.

facts.fact: Under the 2021 IFGC, masonry chimneys serving residential-type and low-heat gas appliances must be lined with clay flue lining (ASTM C315), a listed chimney lining system (UL 1777), or another approved material that resists flue gases and condensate at temperatures up to 1,800 F.

Under the 2021 IFGC, when a masonry chimney that served solid or liquid fuel is reused for gas, it must be cleaned and must have an accessible cleanout with a tight-fitting noncombustible cover, with the upper edge of the cleanout at least 6 inches below the lowest chimney inlet.

IFGC 2021 503.5.5: a chimney serving one draft-hood appliance must have an effective area at least equal to the draft hood outlet (or flue collar) area and no more than 7 times that area. For two draft-hood appliances, the area must be at least the larger outlet area plus 50 percent of the smaller, and no more than 7 times the smallest outlet area.

Under the 2021 IFGC, Category II and III appliances use special gas vents listed to UL 1738, installed per the vent manufacturer's instructions (Type B and BW vents are UL 441). Plastic vent pipe for Category IV appliances need not be listed if the appliance manufacturer specifies it, and any required primer must be a contrasting color so joints can be inspected.

IFGC 2021 503.3.3: mechanical draft systems must be listed to UL 378. Parts under positive pressure must be built to keep flue gas from leaking into the building, a natural-draft vent connector may not connect to a positive-pressure section, and gas to the main burners must shut off if the draft system is not working properly.

IFGC 2021 503.6.10.2: Type B and L vents sized by the draft-hood-area method must run generally vertical with offsets of 45 degrees or less (one 60-degree offset is allowed; anything steeper counts as horizontal), and the total horizontal run of the vent plus connector may not exceed 75 percent of the vent's vertical height.

IFGC 2021 503.6.14: screws and rivets may not penetrate the inner wall of a double-wall (Type B) gas vent, except at the transition from the appliance draft hood outlet, flue collar or single-wall connector to the double-wall vent.

IFGC 2021 503.7: single-wall metal pipe used as a vent must be galvanized steel at least 0.0304 inch thick (or equivalent), extend at least 5 ft above the highest draft hood or flue collar and at least 2 ft above the roof and anything within 10 ft, and run directly from the appliance space through the roof or an exterior wall. It may not start in or pass through an attic, inside wall, concealed space or floor, and uninsulated pipe may not be used outdoors where the 99 percent winter design temperature is below 32 F.

IFGC 2021 503.7.7: single-wall vent pipe passing through a combustible exterior wall needs a ventilated metal thimble at least 4 in larger in diameter than the pipe for listed draft-hood appliances (2 in larger if at least 6 ft of pipe is exposed before the thimble), 6 in larger for unlisted draft-hood appliances, and 12 in larger for residential and low-heat appliances.

IFGC 2021 503.10.2.3: vent connectors for residential-type appliances that are not Type B or L must be galvanized steel at least 0.018 inch thick, aluminum (1100 or 3003 alloy) at least 0.027 inch, stainless steel at least 0.012 inch, or a listed connector, and connectors may not be wrapped in insulation unless listed as insulated.

IFGC 2021 Table 503.10.5 single-wall vent connector clearances to combustibles: 6 in for listed draft-hood appliances, 9 in for residential boilers and furnaces with a listed conversion burner and draft hood, 18 in for other residential and low-heat appliances, and 36 in for medium-heat appliances.

Under the 2021 IFGC, the whole length of a vent connector must be readily accessible for inspection, cleaning and replacement (503.10.12), and single-wall connectors may not pass through any wall, floor or ceiling except as allowed for single-wall vents in 503.7.4 (503.10.14).

Under the 2021 IFGC, a draft hood must be in the same room as the appliance's combustion air supply so no pressure difference exists (503.12.5), and its relief opening must be at least 6 inches from any surface other than the appliance and its vent, unless the appliance label requires more (503.12.7).

Under the 2021 IFGC, manually operated dampers may not be placed in vent connectors (fixed baffles are not considered dampers), automatically operated vent dampers must be listed, and no device that slows vent gas flow may be installed in a connector, vent or chimney except listed draft regulators, listed heat reclaimers, listed automatic dampers and similar approved devices.

Under the 2021 IFGC, an unvented room heater may not be the only source of comfort heat in a dwelling unit (621.2), may not exceed 40,000 Btu/h input (621.3), and may not be installed in Group A, E or I occupancies (621.4).

IFGC 2021 621.6: unvented room heaters must have an oxygen-depletion safety shutoff that cuts gas to the main and pilot burners when oxygen drops to the manufacturer's set point, which may not be lower than 18 percent oxygen, and it may not be adjustable in the field.

IFGC 2021 623.7: a domestic gas range needs at least 30 inches of vertical clearance between the cooking top and combustible material or metal cabinets above. It may be reduced to 24 inches with 1/4 inch insulating millboard covered by sheet metal at least 0.0122 inch thick, a metal ventilating hood (0.0122 inch) with a 1/4 inch air space that is at least as wide as the range and centered, or a listed microwave or other appliance installed per its instructions.

IFGC 2021 620.4: unless listed for less, a suspended gas unit heater needs 18 in clearance at the sides, 12 in at the bottom and 6 in above the top (with an internal draft hood), and a floor-mounted unit heater needs 6 in to combustibles at the back and one side.

IFGC 2021 630.3: where unvented infrared radiant heaters are used, outdoor ventilation air of at least 4 cfm per 1,000 Btu/h of total heater input must be provided, with flue product exhaust openings located above the heaters. Example: 150,000 Btu/h of unvented infrared heaters needs at least 600 cfm.
IFGC 2021 625.1: a gas refrigerator without manufacturer's clearance instructions needs at least 2 inches between its back and the wall and at least 12 inches above the top.

Under the 2021 IFGC (and IMC 909), no door may swing within 12 inches of a vented wall furnace's air inlet or outlet, measured at right angles to the opening, and doorstops or door closers may not be used to meet this. Ducts may not be attached to a wall furnace, and a wall furnace between a bathroom and another room may not circulate bathroom air.

Under the 2021 IFGC, floor furnaces may not be placed in doorways, stair landings, aisles, passageways or exits, or in concrete floors built on grade. A horizontal floor register must be at least 6 in from the nearest wall, and doors, draperies or similar items must be at least 12 in from the register.

Under the 2021 IFGC, the lowest part of a floor furnace must be at least 6 inches above the ground (2 inches if the lower 6 inches are sealed by the manufacturer against water); otherwise a pit is excavated, with at least 12 inches of clearance on all sides and 18 inches on the control side.

IFGC 2021 618.3: outdoor or return air for a forced-air furnace may not be taken from a room whose volume is less than 25 percent of the total volume served by the system (spaces joined by permanent openings count together). The rule does not apply where the return air taken from the room is no more than the supply air delivered to it.

IFGC 2021 618.3: a room containing a fuel-burning appliance may not be the only source of return air unless the appliance is direct-vent, or the room volume exceeds 1 cubic foot per 10 Btu/h of total appliance input, supply and return air are about equal, and return inlets are at least 10 ft from any draft hood or atmospheric burner. Example: a 100,000 Btu/h furnace needs a room larger than 10,000 cubic feet.

Under the 2021 IFGC, return air from one dwelling unit may not be discharged into another dwelling unit (618.5). When a furnace's supply ducts serve areas outside the room it sits in, its return air must come through ducts sealed to the furnace casing and ending outside that room (618.6).

IFGC 2021 627.8: a cooling coil must be installed in parallel with, or downstream (on the outlet side) of, a gas furnace unless the furnace is listed for use with an upstream coil, and the coil must not overload the blower's capacity. Condensate must be kept off the heating element.
Under the 2021 IFGC and IMC, a clothes dryer exhaust terminal must keep the duct passageway undiminished and provide an open area of at least 12.5 square inches.

Under the 2021 IFGC and IMC, wherever a space for a clothes dryer is provided, a dryer exhaust duct must be installed; if no dryer is installed at occupancy, the duct must be capped at the dryer location. Exception: a listed condensing (ductless) dryer installed before occupancy.

IFGC 2021 614.10: exhaust ducts for Type 2 (commercial) clothes dryers need at least 6 inches of clearance to combustible materials, the exhaust fan motor must be outside the airstream, and where several dryers share a duct the fan must run continuously or be interlocked with the dryers.

Under 40 CFR 82.152, a small appliance is a product that is fully manufactured, charged and hermetically sealed in a factory with 5 pounds or less of refrigerant, such as household refrigerators and freezers, room air conditioners, dehumidifiers and drinking water coolers. Servicing small appliances requires Type I (or Universal) certification.

Under 40 CFR 82.152, an appliance's full charge (the amount needed for normal operation) may be determined by: the manufacturer's specified charge; a calculation from component sizes, refrigerant density and piping volume; actual measurements of refrigerant added or removed (including seasonal adjustments); or the midpoint of an established range based on the best available operating data.

EPA appliance categories (40 CFR 82.152): comfort cooling is air conditioning that controls heat or humidity in occupied buildings (such as chillers, commercial split systems and rooftop units); commercial refrigeration serves the retail food and cold storage warehouse sectors; industrial process refrigeration is customized equipment tied to industrial processes, ice rinks and industrial ice machines. A dual-use appliance counts as industrial process refrigeration if at least half its capacity serves industrial processes.

An MVAC-like appliance (40 CFR 82.152) is an open-drive compressor system with a full charge of 20 pounds or less used to cool the cab of off-road vehicles such as farm or construction equipment (R-22 units excluded). Under 82.161(a), technicians servicing MVAC-like appliances must hold Type II certification or Section 609 (Subpart B) certification, while regular motor vehicle AC requires Section 609 certification.

Under 40 CFR 82.152, a technician is anyone whose work could reasonably be expected to break into the refrigerant circuit, such as attaching or detaching hoses and gauges, adding or removing refrigerant, adding or removing components, or cutting lines; painting or tightening bolts does not count. Connecting hoses and gauges to measure pressure, add refrigerant or recover refrigerant is not considered 'opening' the appliance.

EPA defines self-contained recovery equipment as equipment that can remove refrigerant without help from the appliance's own components (it has its own compressor or pump), and system-dependent (passive) recovery equipment as equipment that needs the appliance's own compressor or pressure to remove the refrigerant.

Under 40 CFR 82.152, a leak inspection must find where leaks are, using methods such as bubble tests, ultrasonic tests, gas-imaging cameras or properly maintained electronic leak detectors. Methods that only show that a leak exists (such as a pressure decay test or checking the sight glass) must be paired with a method that locates the leak.

Under 40 CFR 82.161(a), an apprentice does not need EPA 608 certification while closely and continually supervised by a certified technician during any work that could release refrigerant; the supervising technician and apprentice share responsibility for compliance. People who only dispose of small appliances, MVACs or MVAC-like appliances do not need to be certified.

Under 40 CFR 82 Subpart F Appendix D, Universal certification can be earned on one combined test or by combining passing scores on separate Type I, II and III tests, but a mail-in Type I test cannot count toward Universal. Results must be sent within 30 days, and a wallet card must be issued within 30 days showing the program's name, the technician's name, the certification type and a unique number that is not the Social Security number.

Under 40 CFR 82.161(b), since January 1, 2018 each approved certification program must publish online a list of technicians it has certified on or after January 1, 2017 (name, city, certification type and date), updated at least yearly, and must let technicians opt out of the list.

Other exceptions to the EPA refrigerant sales restriction (40 CFR 82.154(c)(1)) include: sales intended only for resale to certified technicians or appliance manufacturers (for example, to a wholesaler), sales to appliance manufacturers, refrigerant contained in an appliance with a fully assembled refrigerant circuit or in an appliance component, and refrigerant charged into an appliance by a certified technician or apprentice during service.

Under 40 CFR 82.154(g), the refrigerant sales restriction has been stayed (not enforced) since April 27, 1995 as it applies to refrigerant contained in appliances without fully assembled refrigerant circuits, such as pre-charged split-system components, while EPA reconsiders the rule.

Under 40 CFR 82.154(c)(2), small cans (2 pounds or less) of non-exempt substitute refrigerant for motor vehicle AC made or imported on or after January 1, 2018 must have a single self-sealing valve that closes automatically and leaks no more than 3.00 grams per year when closed, tested by an independent U.S. laboratory.

Under 40 CFR 82.154(e), appliances (other than small appliances) must be built with a servicing aperture, and small appliances with a process stub, so refrigerant can be removed during service and disposal. Under 82.154(f), one-time expansion devices (such as self-chilling cans) may not be made or imported unless they use only exempt refrigerants.

Under 40 CFR 82.156(a)(1)(iii), before opening an appliance just to change the compressor oil, the technician must evacuate or pressurize the appliance (or isolated section) to no higher than 5 psig, or drain the oil into a system receiver that has been evacuated or pressurized to no higher than 5 psig.

Under 40 CFR 82.156(a)(1)(ii), for a non-major repair, a low-pressure appliance must be pressurized to no higher than 0 psig before opening. For refrigerants that boil above 85 F at 29.9 in. Hg (such as R-123), heat should be used to raise the pressure, and nitrogen may be used only to raise the pressure from the level heat can reach up to atmospheric.

Under 40 CFR 82.156(a), technicians may evacuate the whole appliance or only the part being serviced if it can be isolated to a system receiver, and they must verify that the required evacuation level has been reached before opening the appliance.

Under 40 CFR 82.156(c) and (d), when MVACs and MVAC-like appliances are disposed of, the refrigerant must be recovered per Subpart B or the system pressure reduced to 102 mm of mercury vacuum or lower.

Under 40 CFR 82.156(h), recovered refrigerant may be charged back into the same appliance or another appliance owned by the same person without being recycled or reclaimed (not allowed for MVAC or MVAC-like appliances). Selling it to a different owner requires reclamation to AHRI 700 purity by a certified reclaimer.

Under 40 CFR 82.157(d), a certified technician must inspect to locate the leaks, and the repair must bring the leak rate below the threshold. A repair is presumed successful if no refrigerant has to be added for 12 months or if later leak inspections find no leaks.

Under 40 CFR 82.157(f), the 30-day (or 120-day) leak repair deadline may be extended if the appliance is in a radiologically contaminated area, other laws make timely repair impossible, or needed parts are unavailable. A parts extension runs until 30 days after the part is delivered, capped at 180 days (270 days with an industrial process shutdown), and EPA must be notified within the original repair period.

Under 40 CFR 82.157(g), an automatic leak detection system can replace the required periodic leak inspections for the parts it monitors if it is audited or calibrated yearly. Refrigerant-in-air sensors must detect 10 ppm and alarm at 100 ppm; other systems must alarm at a loss of 50 lb or 10 percent of the full charge, whichever is less.

Under 40 CFR 82.157(h), a retrofit or retirement plan must be signed by an authorized official, dated, kept at the site, and include the appliance identity and location, refrigerant type and charge, the planned conversion or disposal, and a schedule of no more than one year. The work must be finished within one year of the plan date and no more than 13 months after the plan was required.

Under 40 CFR 82.157, owners may get 18 months to retire an appliance if its replacement uses an exempt substitute refrigerant (82.157(i)); repair and retrofit deadlines are suspended while an appliance is mothballed and restart when refrigerant is added back; and refrigerant purged and destroyed at 98 percent or greater efficiency does not count toward the leak rate (82.157(k)).

Under the HFC leak repair rule (40 CFR 84.106, effective January 1, 2026), owners calculate the leak rate each time refrigerant is added using either the annualizing method or the rolling average method (the same method at all their facilities). After an exceedance, commercial refrigeration and industrial process systems of 500 lb or more get quarterly leak inspections, while those of 15 to under 500 lb and comfort cooling systems get annual inspections, and any appliance of 15 lb or more that leaks 125 percent of its charge in a year must be reported to EPA by March 1.

The 40 CFR 84.106 HFC leak repair rule does not apply to appliances that contain only an ozone-depleting refrigerant (those stay under 40 CFR 82.157) or to residential and light commercial air conditioning and heat pumps. Refrigerated transport falls in the 10 percent leak-rate group with comfort cooling.

Under 40 CFR 84.108, required automatic leak detection on 1,500 lb or larger commercial and industrial process refrigeration systems must be audited and calibrated yearly; direct-detection sensors must detect 10 ppm and alarm at 100 ppm, condition-monitoring systems must alarm at a loss of 50 lb or 10 percent of the charge (whichever is less), and after an alarm the owner has 30 days (120 with a shutdown) to calculate the leak rate or repair the leak.

Under 40 CFR 84.54(c)(1), since January 1, 2025 new residential and light commercial AC and heat pump systems (other than VRF) may not be installed with a refrigerant of GWP 700 or more, except that systems whose specified components were all manufactured or imported before January 1, 2025 may still be installed. After the May 26, 2026 amendment, the text sets no deadline for installing those older-component systems.

Under 40 CFR 84.54(c)(2), new residential and light commercial variable refrigerant flow (VRF) systems may not be installed with refrigerant of GWP 700 or more starting January 1, 2026, except that VRF systems with all components made or imported before January 1, 2026 may be installed until January 1, 2027 (January 1, 2028 with a building permit approved before October 5, 2023).

Under 40 CFR 84.54(a), since January 1, 2025 self-contained residential and light commercial AC and heat pumps, residential dehumidifiers and comfort-cooling chillers may not be manufactured or imported with refrigerant of GWP 700 or more, and household refrigerators and freezers are limited to GWP below 150. Under 84.54(b), selling or distributing such products is restricted starting three years after the manufacture date.

The AIM Act (42 U.S.C. 7675(e)(2)(C)) phases down U.S. HFC production and consumption, measured against a baseline in exchange-value-weighted amounts: 90 percent of baseline for 2020-2023, 60 percent for 2024-2028, 30 percent for 2029-2033, 20 percent for 2034-2035, and 15 percent for 2036 and later (an 85 percent cut).

IMC 2021 Table 305.4 maximum hanger spacing: copper or copper-alloy tubing 8 ft horizontal and 10 ft vertical; copper pipe 12 ft horizontal and 10 ft vertical; steel pipe 12 ft horizontal and 15 ft vertical; PVC pipe 4 ft horizontal and 10 ft vertical (with a mid-story guide); PEX 1 inch and smaller 32 inches horizontal and 10 ft vertical.
facts.note: Confirmed in Seattle's published 2021 Mechanical Code (IMC text; Washington does not amend IMC 305).

facts.fact: IMC 2021 Table 403.3.1.1: retail sales floors use a default of 15 people per 1,000 sq ft with 7.5 cfm per person plus 0.12 cfm per sq ft. Example: a 2,000 sq ft store with 30 people needs (7.5 x 30) + (0.12 x 2,000) = 225 + 240 = 465 cfm of breathing-zone outdoor air.
facts.note: Values match ASHRAE 62.1 Table 6.2.2.1, which the IMC table is based on.

facts.fact: IMC 2021 Table 403.3.1.1: restaurant dining rooms use 70 people per 1,000 sq ft, and cafeterias/fast-food dining and bars/cocktail lounges use 100 people per 1,000 sq ft; all three require 7.5 cfm per person plus 0.18 cfm per sq ft of outdoor air.

IMC 2021 Table 403.3.1.1: conference and meeting rooms use 50 people per 1,000 sq ft, and auditorium seating 150 people per 1,000 sq ft, both at 5 cfm per person plus 0.06 cfm per sq ft. Classrooms for ages 5 to 8 use 25 people per 1,000 sq ft at 10 cfm per person plus 0.12 cfm per sq ft.

IMC 2021 Table 403.3.1.1 exhaust rates include: commercial cooking kitchens 0.7 cfm per sq ft, janitor closets 1.0 cfm per sq ft, locker rooms 0.5 cfm per sq ft, and enclosed parking garages 0.75 cfm per sq ft. Commercial kitchens also need 7.5 cfm per person plus 0.12 cfm per sq ft of outdoor air (default 20 people per 1,000 sq ft).

Under the IMC (Section 404), enclosed parking garage ventilation may cycle or modulate under automatic detection controls, but automatic operation may never reduce the rate below 0.05 cfm per sq ft of floor area, and the system must be able to provide 0.75 cfm per sq ft.
facts.note: The 2024 IMC 404.1 requires carbon monoxide detectors used together with nitrogen dioxide detectors (listed to UL 2075) when the system is not run continuously.

facts.fact: IMC 2021 403.2.1 limits recirculation: ventilation air may not be recirculated from one dwelling unit to another or to dissimilar occupancies; pool and pool-deck air may be recirculated only if dehumidified to 60 percent relative humidity or less; and spaces that require mechanical exhaust under Note b of Table 403.3.1.1 (such as toilet rooms) may not have their air recirculated, so all air supplied to them must be exhausted.

facts.source: IMC 2021 Sec. 403.3.1.1 (zone air distribution effectiveness table)
facts.fact: Additional IMC zone air distribution effectiveness (Ez) values: 0.7 for warm air supplied at the floor with a ceiling return, and 0.5 when makeup air is drawn in near the exhaust or return. Lower Ez means more outdoor air: Voz = Vbz / Ez, so 100 cfm / 0.7 = about 143 cfm.
facts.note: Values agree with ASHRAE 62.1 Table 6.2.2.2.

facts.fact: IMC 2021 601.4: exhaust ducts under positive pressure, chimneys and vents may not extend into or pass through supply or return ducts or plenums (limited exceptions apply, such as positive-pressure vents listed for the use with no joints in the plenum or run inside a sealed conduit).

IMC 2021 601.5 and IRC 2021 M1602.2: return air openings must be at least 10 ft (in any direction) from an open combustion chamber or draft hood of another appliance in the same room, the return air taken from a room may not exceed the supply air delivered to that room, and return openings are sized per the manufacturer, ACCA Manual D or the design professional.

IRC 2021 M1602.2 also prohibits taking return air from an unconditioned crawl space by a direct connection to the furnace return (transfer openings in the crawl space enclosure are allowed), and return air from one dwelling unit may not be discharged into another dwelling unit.

In the 2021 IMC Table 603.4 (single dwelling units) and IRC Table M1601.1.1, minimum galvanized steel thickness depends on size and pressure: round ducts under 12 in at 1/2 in. w.c. need 0.013 in, 15-17 in round need 0.016 in, rectangular ducts 8 in or less need 0.013 in, 13-16 in rectangular need 0.019 in, and 19-20 in rectangular need 0.024 in. Ducts over 20 in or over 1 in. w.c. must follow SMACNA.

Under the 2021 IMC and IRC, crimp joints in round metal ducts must have a contact lap of at least 1 inch with the male end pointing in the direction of airflow, and must be mechanically fastened with at least three sheet metal screws or rivets equally spaced around the joint.

IMC 2021 603.3: ducts are classified by design static pressure in pressure classes of +/-0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 10 in. w.c., and the duct's class must equal or exceed the system's design operating pressure.

Under the 2021 IMC and IRC, underground ducts must be approved for that use; metal ducts without corrosion protection must be fully encased in at least 2 inches of concrete; ducts must slope to an accessible point for drainage (IMC: at least 1/8 inch per foot); plastic underground ducts are limited to 150 F; and ducts must be sealed, secured and tested before burial.

IMC 2021 603.18: supply and return outlets need volume dampers or another means of adjustment, floor registers must resist a 200 lb load on a 2-inch-diameter disc, and registers may not be installed in the floor of toilet and bathing rooms with hard nonabsorbent floors (except in dwelling units).

Under the 2021 IRC, vibration isolators between ducts and equipment may be no longer than 10 inches (M1601.2); factory-made air ducts may not be installed in or on the ground, in tile or metal pipe, or within masonry or concrete (M1601.4.7); and ducts must be at least 4 inches from earth unless built as underground ducts (M1601.4.8).

Under the 2021 IRC M1601.5, under-floor (crawl space) supply plenums are not allowed in new structures. Where an existing one is modified, the furnace fan must start at 150 F or lower with a separate limit holding outlet air to 200 F, the access opening must be at least 18 by 24 inches, and the ground needs a vapor barrier of at least 4 mils.

Under the 2021 IMC (604.7) and IRC (M1601.3), external duct insulation and factory-insulated flexible duct must be printed or identified at intervals of no more than 36 inches with the manufacturer's name, the installed R-value, and the flame spread and smoke-developed indexes.
facts.note: An earlier KB entry stated 10 ft; the 2021 IMC and IRC text both say 36 inches.

facts.fact: IMC 2021 604.2: ducts that operate above 120 F must have enough insulation to keep their exposed surface temperature at or below 120 F.

Under the 2021 IMC and IRC, externally insulated cooling ducts that pass through spaces where condensation can form need a vapor retarder of 0.05 perm or less (or aluminum foil at least 2 mils thick) over the insulation, with sealed joints.
facts.note: Spray polyurethane foam rated 3 perms per inch or less is an exception.

facts.fact: Under the 2021 IMC, duct liner must be interrupted at fire damper operating areas and for at least 6 inches upstream and downstream of electric or fuel-fired heaters in the duct (604.8), and water-permeable internal insulation may not be used from the cooling coil outlet to the downstream end of the drain pan (604.13).

Under the 2021 IMC, HVAC systems need approved air filters located in the return or outdoor air stream upstream of any heat exchanger or coil (605.1). Media filters are listed to UL 900, HEPA filters to UL 586 and electrostatic filters to UL 867, but filters used inside dwelling units need not be listed (605.2). Ducts must spread air evenly across the whole filter face (605.3).
facts.note: Washington amends 605.1 and adds MERV minimums; the UL listing standards are model IMC text.

facts.fact: IMC 2021 607.3.3.1: a fire damper's heat-responsive device must operate at about 50 F above the normal temperature in the duct, but not lower than 160 F; in a smoke control system it may be rated up to 350 F.

Under the 2021 IMC, fire and smoke dampers with fusible links or internal operators need an access door at least 12 inches square or a removable duct section (607.4), and flexible air ducts and flexible air connectors may not pass through any fire-resistance-rated assembly (607.7).

IMC 2021 607.6.1 exception: in a dwelling, a duct may pass through up to three floors without fire dampers if it is inside a wall cavity, made of steel at least 0.0187 inch (No. 26 gage), serves only one dwelling or sleeping unit, is no larger than 4 inches nominal diameter, and the total of such ducts is no more than 100 sq in per 100 sq ft of floor area.

Under the 2021 IMC, cooling towers, evaporative condensers and fluid coolers must be located so the plume discharges at least 5 ft above or 20 ft away from any ventilation inlet to a building (908.1), and their drains and blowdown must be indirectly connected to an approved disposal location (908.6).

IMC 2021 914 (sauna heaters): the thermostat must limit room temperature to 194 F (sensor within 6 inches of the ceiling if not built in), the timer may allow no more than 1 hour of operation with its control outside the sauna room, and the room needs a ventilation opening at least 4 by 8 inches near the top of the door.

IMC 2021 Table 1103.1 lists the most refrigerant allowed in a single circuit per 1,000 cubic feet of occupied space before a machinery room (or outdoor location) is needed: R-22 13 lb, R-134a 13 lb, R-407C 18 lb, R-410A 26 lb, R-404A 31 lb, R-32 4.8 lb, R-290 (propane) 0.56 lb and R-123 3.5 lb.
facts.note: R-22, R-134a, R-407C, R-410A and R-404A confirmed in 2018 IMC text and Seattle's current code; R-32, R-290 and R-123 from Seattle's current Chapter 11. All match ASHRAE 34 RCL values.

facts.fact: Worked example using IMC Table 1103.1: an R-32 system serving a 12 x 12 x 8 ft room (1,152 cubic feet) may hold at most 4.8 x 1,152 / 1,000 = about 5.5 lb in a single circuit; the same room with R-410A (26 lb per 1,000 cubic feet) could hold about 30 lb.

Under IMC 2021 1102.2, refrigerants with different ASHRAE 34 designations may not be mixed in a system (except an additive the manufacturer permits for oil return). Refrigerant added to a system must be new, recovered (reused only in the same owner's systems after filtering and drying; visibly contaminated refrigerant must be reclaimed), or reclaimed to AHRI 700 purity for use by a different owner.

IMC 2021 1101.8: before changing the type of refrigerant in a circuit holding more than 220 lb of a Group A1 refrigerant or more than 30 lb of any other group, the owner must notify the code official, and the new refrigerant must comply with the code.
facts.note: Section number per the 2018/2021 IMC layout; Seattle's current Chapter 11, which follows the newer 2024-style layout, numbers it 1101.7.

facts.fact: IMC 2021 1104.2 exception: listed equipment containing 6.6 lb (3 kg) or less of refrigerant, installed per its listing and the manufacturer's instructions, does not need a machinery room no matter what the refrigerant's safety classification is.

Under the 2021 IMC, where a device with an open flame or a surface hotter than 800 F is in a room holding more than 6.6 lb of refrigerant in a single circuit, a hood and exhaust system per Section 510 is required (1104.3.4), and machinery rooms may not contain permanently installed open-flame devices or continuously hot surfaces above 800 F (1106.2).

Under the 2021 IMC, refrigeration machinery room exhaust must discharge outdoors at least 20 ft from property lines and building openings (1105.6.1), and pressure relief devices must discharge at least 15 ft above adjoining grade and at least 20 ft from any window, ventilation opening or exit (1105.7).

IMC 2021 1105.6.3.1: normal ventilation of an occupied refrigeration machinery room is the greatest of 0.5 cfm per sq ft, the airflow needed to hold the room's temperature rise to 18 F, or 20 cfm per person. When unoccupied it may drop to the greater of 0.25 cfm per sq ft or the 18 F temperature-rise airflow, with controls that raise it when the room lights are on.

Under the 2021 IMC, refrigerant piping that crosses an open space used as a passageway must be at least 7 ft 3 in above the floor unless it is run against the ceiling (1107.2), and refrigerant piping installed in a concrete floor must be encased in a pipe duct (1107.2.1).
facts.note: Seattle's current Chapter 11, which follows the newer 2024-style layout, numbers these 1109.2.1 and 1109.2.4.

facts.fact: Under the 2021 IMC, systems with positive-displacement compressors holding more than 6.6 lb of refrigerant need stop valves at each compressor (or condensing unit) inlet and discharge and at each liquid receiver outlet (1107.8); systems with 100 lb or more also need a stop valve at each liquid receiver inlet (1107.8.1). Self-contained systems are among the exceptions.

Under the 2021 IMC, field-erected systems using copper tubing no larger than 5/8 inch OD may be tested with the system's own refrigerant charged to its saturated vapor pressure at 70 F or higher instead of a separate pressure test (1108.1 exception), and systems holding 55 lb or more of refrigerant need a signed test certificate stating the refrigerant and the high- and low-side test pressures (1108.4).

facts.source: 2024 IMC Chapter 11 (as adopted in Seattle Mechanical Code Ch. 11, Sec. 1109.3)
facts.fact: The 2024 IMC adds A2L/B2L piping rules: tubing for these refrigerants that is less than 1-1/2 inches from the edge of a stud or joist needs a steel shield plate at least 0.0575 inch (No. 16 gage), and a naturally ventilated shaft carrying the piping needs a vent pipe at least 4 inches in diameter from the lowest point to outdoors.
facts.note: Seen in Seattle's adopted Chapter 11, which follows the 2024 IMC layout; not confirmed against the 2024 IMC text itself. Not in the 2021 IMC.

facts.fact: Under the 2021 IRC, piping embedded in a radiant floor heating system must be rated for at least 80 psi at 180 F (M2103.1), and it must be hydrostatically tested at not less than 100 psi for 30 minutes, with every joint visually checked for leaks (M2103.4).

Under the 2021 IRC, joints in hydronic piping embedded in concrete must be: welded for steel, brazed for copper tubing (not soldered), heat-fused for polybutylene and polypropylene, solvent cemented for CPVC, and cold-expansion, insert or compression type for PEX.

Under the 2021 IRC, where a hydronic system's pressure is reduced (for example, by a pressure-reducing valve), a relief valve must be installed on the low-pressure side and set at the system's maximum design pressure (M2101.23), and hydronic pipe whose surface exceeds 250 F needs at least 1 inch of clearance to combustible materials (M2101.27).

Under the 2021 IRC, ground-source heat pump loop piping entering a building must be marked 'GROUND-SOURCE HEAT-PUMP LOOP SYSTEM' with any antifreeze and its concentration named (M2105.25). After the 100 psi, 15-minute test, the measured flow rate and pressure drop are compared to design values, and a difference of more than 10 percent must be found and corrected (M2105.28).

IRC 2021 Table M2003.2 sizes hot water heating expansion tanks by system volume: a 50 gallon system needs a 4.0 gallon diaphragm (pressurized) tank or a 7.5 gallon nonpressurized tank, and a 100 gallon system needs 8.0 or 15.0 gallons. The table assumes 195 F average water, 12 psig fill and 30 psig maximum operating pressure, and pressurized tanks must withstand a hydrostatic test of 2-1/2 times the system's allowable working pressure.
facts.note: Seattle strikes this IRC section because it regulates boilers under a local boiler code; the values shown are the 2021 IRC text.

facts.fact: IRC 2021 M2002.4: the discharge from a boiler's pressure-relief valve must be piped by gravity to within 18 inches of the floor or to an open receptor.

IRC 2021 M1401.3 lets equipment exceed the Manual S size limits only where (1) multistage or variable-capacity (VRF) equipment has a published capacity range that covers the calculated loads, or (2) no published capacity meets both the total and sensible loads and the next larger standard size is used.

IRC 2021 M1407: an electric duct heater installed within 4 ft of a heat pump or air conditioner must be listed for that installation (and the heat pump or AC must be listed for it too), and duct heaters must be interlocked so they cannot run unless the system fan is running.

IRC 2021 M1411.2: where a cooling coil is placed in the supply plenum of a warm-air furnace, the furnace blower must be rated for at least 0.5 in. w.c. static pressure unless the furnace is listed for use with a cooling coil, and cooling coils may not be placed upstream of the heat exchanger unless listed for it.

Under the 2021 IRC, refrigerant suction lines must be insulated to at least R-3 with an external surface permeance of no more than 0.05 perm (M1411.6), and refrigerant piping installed within 1-1/2 inches of the underside of roof decking must be protected from roofing nails and fasteners (M1411.7).

ACCA manuals: Manual J = residential load calculation, Manual S = residential equipment selection, Manual D = residential duct design, Manual T = air distribution basics (choosing supply outlets and returns to avoid drafts and stagnant air), Manual N = commercial load calculation, Manual Q = commercial low-pressure duct design, Manual Zr = residential zoning, Manual B = testing, adjusting and balancing, Manual H = heat pump systems, and Manual P = psychrometrics. Manuals J and D are ANSI-approved standards.

facts.source: DOE 10 CFR 430 Appendix M1; NYSERDA Clean Heat fact sheet (cleanheatconnect.ny.gov)
facts.fact: DOE's Appendix M1 test procedure (for units made on or after January 1, 2023) raised the external static pressure used to rate ducted systems from about 0.1-0.2 in. w.c. to 0.5 in. w.c., which is why SEER2, EER2 and HSPF2 numbers are lower than the old SEER, EER and HSPF. There is no single conversion factor; for example, the 2023 split heat pump minimum of 14.3 SEER2 / 7.5 HSPF2 corresponds to 15 SEER / 8.8 HSPF in the old metrics.

facts.source: ACHR News, Testing the Run Capacitor While the System Is Running; ACCA HVAC Blog
facts.fact: A run capacitor can be checked under load with: microfarads = (2,652 x amps) / volts, using the current on the wire from the capacitor's HERM (or FAN) terminal and the voltage measured across the capacitor terminals. Example: 4.0 A at 380 V gives 2,652 x 4 / 380 = about 27.9 uF; compare it to the rated value (many run capacitors allow about +/-6 percent).
facts.note: ACCA's blog rounds the constant to 2,650.

facts.source: IAEI Magazine, Air Conditioning Equipment Installations; NEC 2023 440.33
facts.fact: Manufacturers figure nameplate minimum circuit ampacity (MCA) as 125 percent of the largest motor-compressor rated-load current plus the other loads (NEC 440.33). Example: a 16 A RLA compressor and a 1.2 A condenser fan give 1.25 x 16 + 1.2 = 21.2 A MCA.

Under NEC 440.22(A), the branch-circuit fuse or breaker for a hermetic motor-compressor may not exceed 175 percent of its rated-load current, and may be raised to no more than 225 percent if the motor will not start. Example: a 16 A RLA compressor allows 28 A, or up to 36 A if needed to start. The equipment nameplate MOCP must never be exceeded (NEC 110.3(B)).

facts.source: Arkema Forane tech tip (A2L vs A1 cylinders); ACCA HVAC Blog (gray A2L cylinders)
facts.fact: Cylinders for A2L refrigerants (such as R-454B and R-32) have a left-hand threaded valve outlet (an AHRI guideline adopted by most manufacturers) so A1 and A2L hoses are not mixed up, a red band or red top marking flammability (a DOT requirement), and a spring-loaded relief valve that recloses instead of a rupture disc.

facts.source: Beckett Corp., Clocking the Gas Meter (burner tutorial)
facts.fact: To clock a gas meter, shut off all other gas appliances, run the appliance at high fire, and time one revolution of the test dial: CFH = 3,600 x dial size (cubic feet) / seconds per revolution, and input (Btu/h) = CFH x the gas heating value. Example: a 1/2 cubic foot dial taking 36 seconds gives 3,600 x 0.5 / 36 = 50 CFH, or about 50,000 Btu/h with 1,000 Btu per cubic foot gas.
facts.note: Get the actual heating value from the gas supplier; it is lower at high altitude.

facts.source: Thermo King service manual, Pressure Rise Test; HVAC School, Vacuum: Moisture vs System Leak
facts.fact: After evacuation, isolate the vacuum pump and watch the micron gauge (decay or pressure-rise test): if pressure rises and then levels off below atmospheric, the system is tight but still wet and needs more evacuation; if it keeps rising toward atmospheric pressure, there is a leak that must be found and repaired.

facts.source: HVAC School, Oil Best Practices for HFC and HFO Systems; RefrigerantHQ, Understanding Refrigerant Oils
facts.fact: Mineral oil is used with older CFC and HCFC refrigerants such as R-12 and R-22 and does not mix well with HFCs, while stationary HFC and HFO systems (such as R-410A and R-404A) use POE oil (PVE in some ductless/VRF units). POE absorbs moisture quickly from the air, so it should only be used from sealed metal containers; water breaks POE down into acids.
facts.note: Automotive R-134a and R-1234yf systems generally use PAG oil.

facts.fact: IMC 2021 506.3.2.5: before a Type I grease duct is concealed or put into use, a light test must be done by passing a lamp of at least 100 watts through the duct to confirm that all welded and brazed joints are liquid-tight.

Under the 2021 IFGC, a gas appliance vented into a fireplace flue needs a noncombustible seal below the connection and access for flue inspection and cleaning; it may not connect to a factory-built fireplace flue unless the appliance is listed for that use (501.7), and a vent connector may enter a fireplace flue only if the fireplace opening is permanently sealed (503.10.13).

Under 40 CFR 82.152, a seasonal variance is refrigerant removed because of a seasonal change in ambient conditions and later added back (no more than was removed) within one 12-month period; such additions do not require a leak rate calculation. To mothball an appliance means to evacuate it to at least atmospheric pressure and shut it down temporarily.

Under 40 CFR 82.154(a)(1), propane (R-290) is an exempt substitute (not covered by the venting prohibition) only in listed end uses, including household refrigerators and freezers, certain residential and light commercial air conditioning, vending machines, ice machines, water coolers and some retail food equipment; isobutane (R-600a) is exempt in household refrigerators, stand-alone retail units and vending machines.
facts.note: Using a hydrocarbon outside its listed end uses is not exempt.

facts.source: 40 CFR 82 Subpart F, Appendix D(b); D(g)
facts.fact: Under 40 CFR 82 Subpart F Appendix D, proctors must check each test taker's photo ID (such as a driver's license, passport or military ID), and certifying programs must keep records of test takers' names and addresses, scores, and test dates and locations indefinitely unless the records are transferred to another approved program or to EPA.

Under 40 CFR 84.112, starting January 1, 2026 certified reclaimers must label each container of reclaimed HFC refrigerant stating that it contains no more than 15 percent virgin regulated substance, and must keep an electronic certification record for each filled container for three years.

Under current 40 CFR 84.54(c), new supermarket systems may not be installed with refrigerant of GWP 1,400 or more from January 1, 2027; retail food remote condensing units (GWP 1,400) and cold storage warehouses (GWP 700) have a July 27, 2026 installation date; and tighter 150/300 GWP tiers apply to all three starting January 1, 2032.
facts.note: Several of these dates were changed by amendments in 2024-2026; check eCFR for the current text.

facts.fact: IFGC 2021 612: recirculating direct-fired industrial air heaters may be used only in industrial or commercial occupancies, may not serve sleeping quarters or hazardous locations, and must bring in outdoor ventilation air of at least 4 cfm per 1,000 Btu/h of rated input.

Under 40 CFR 82.156(f), people who service only their own appliances that have permanently attached pump-out units are not required to use certified self-contained recovery equipment; elsewhere, system-dependent recovery is limited to appliances with 15 lb or less (82.156(e)).

More IFGC 2021 Table 402.4(2) values (Schedule 40, natural gas, 0.5 in. w.c. drop): at 20 ft, 1/2 in = 118 CFH, 3/4 in = 247, 1 in = 466; at 40 ft, 81, 170 and 320. Example: a 150 CFH load with a 40 ft longest length needs 3/4 in pipe (170 CFH), but a 200 CFH load needs 1 in (320 CFH).

IMC 2021 Table 403.3.1.1: hotel bedrooms and living rooms use 10 people per 1,000 sq ft at 5 cfm per person plus 0.06 cfm per sq ft, and lecture classrooms use 65 people per 1,000 sq ft at 7.5 cfm per person plus 0.06 cfm per sq ft.

Under 40 CFR 82.157(g), required leak inspections cover all visible and accessible components, but need not include components that are insulated, underground, behind walls, iced over or otherwise inaccessible, components more than 2 meters (about 6.5 ft) above the ground, or components site personnel judge unsafe to reach.

Under 40 CFR 82.161(b), EPA encourages certification programs to offer the 608 test in other languages or allow translators, and a program may give an oral test if the candidate makes a written request, explaining the need, at least 30 days before the exam.

IMC 2021 601.2: corridors may not be used as supply, return, exhaust, relief or ventilation air ducts. Limited exceptions apply, such as using corridor air as makeup air for adjoining toilet rooms, bathrooms, dressing rooms and janitor closets when the corridor gets outdoor air at a higher rate than the makeup air taken from it.

IRC 2021 M2105.29: ground-source heat pump loop piping embedded in concrete must be pressure tested before the concrete is poured, and the proposed operating pressure must be maintained in the piping during the pour.

questions.q: Using the longest length method with IFGC Table 402.4(2), the longest run is 60 ft and the main from the meter carries 205 CFH. What is the smallest Schedule 40 main that works?
questions.why: In the 60 ft row, 3/4 in carries only 137 CFH while 1 in carries 257 CFH, so 1 in is the smallest size that handles 205 CFH.

questions.q: Per IFGC 2021 Table 402.4(2) (natural gas, 0.5 in. w.c. drop), what is the capacity of 3/4 in Schedule 40 pipe at 10 ft?
questions.why: At 10 ft the table lists 172 CFH for 1/2 in, 360 CFH for 3/4 in and 678 CFH for 1 in.

questions.q: A branch serves a 150 CFH load and the longest length from the meter is 40 ft. Using IFGC Table 402.4(2), what is the smallest Schedule 40 pipe size?
questions.why: At 40 ft, 1/2 in carries 81 CFH and 3/4 in carries 170 CFH, so 3/4 in is enough for 150 CFH.

questions.q: An appliance requires 36 in of clearance at the sides. Using No. 24 gage sheet metal spaced out 1 in with a ventilated air space (IFGC Table 308.2), the side clearance can be reduced to:
questions.why: Table 308.2 reduces a 36 in required clearance to 12 in at the sides and rear (18 in above) with 24 gage sheet metal and a 1 in air space.

questions.q: Per IFGC 2021 Table 308.2, a 3-1/2 in masonry wall installed with no air space reduces a required 36 in side clearance to:
questions.why: Masonry without an air space reduces 36 in to 24 in at the sides and rear; with a 1 in ventilated air space it reduces to 12 in.

questions.q: Under IFGC 2021 303.7, how far must the side of a pit be held back from the control side of a gas appliance installed in the pit?
questions.why: Pit sides must be at least 12 in from the appliance, and at least 30 in on the control side.

questions.q: Under the 2021 IFGC, how must arc-resistant CSST (ARCSST) be bonded?
c: With a 6 AWG copper jumper to the service grounding electrode system
With a 4 AWG jumper no longer than 50 ft
It is electrically continuous and bonded to an effective ground-fault current path like other gas piping
It does not need to be bonded at all
questions.why: IFGC 2021 310.3 treats arc-resistant CSST like other gas piping; the 6 AWG direct-bond jumper in 310.2 applies to CSST that is not arc-resistant.

questions.q: A room has a volume of 2,000 cubic feet. Under IFGC 501.8 and 621.5, what is the most total input of unvented room heaters allowed in it?
questions.why: The limit is 20 Btu/h per cubic foot of room volume: 2,000 x 20 = 40,000 Btu/h.

questions.q: Under IFGC 2021 503.5.5, the effective area of a chimney serving one draft-hood appliance may not be more than how many times the draft hood outlet area?
questions.why: The chimney area must be at least the draft hood outlet area and no more than 7 times that area, so it is not oversized.

questions.q: For Type B vents sized by the draft-hood method, IFGC 503.6.10.2 limits offsets to 45 degrees from vertical, except that a vent may have:
questions.why: Offsets may not exceed 45 degrees, except one 60-degree offset is allowed; anything steeper counts as horizontal.

questions.q: Under IFGC 2021 503.7, single-wall metal pipe used as a gas vent may NOT:
c: Pass through an attic or concealed space
Run directly through the roof from the appliance room
Be made of galvanized steel at least 0.0304 in thick
questions.why: Single-wall vent pipe must run directly from the appliance space through the roof or exterior wall and may not start in or pass through an attic, inside wall, concealed space or floor.

questions.q: A single-wall vent from a listed draft-hood appliance passes through a combustible exterior wall. Under IFGC 503.7.7, the ventilated metal thimble must normally be how much larger in diameter than the pipe?
questions.why: For listed draft-hood appliances the thimble must be at least 4 in larger (2 in if at least 6 ft of pipe is exposed first); 12 in applies to residential and low-heat appliances.

questions.q: Per IFGC 2021 Table 503.10.5, what clearance to combustibles is required for a single-wall vent connector serving a residential or low-heat appliance (not a listed draft-hood appliance)?
questions.why: The table requires 18 in for single-wall connectors on other residential and low-heat appliances, 6 in for listed draft-hood appliances and 36 in for medium-heat appliances.

questions.q: Under IFGC 2021 503.12.7, a draft hood's relief opening must be at least how far from any surface other than the appliance and its venting system?
questions.why: The relief opening must be at least 6 in from other surfaces unless the appliance label requires more.

questions.q: Under IFGC 2021 621.3, what is the maximum input rating of an unvented room heater?
questions.why: Unvented room heaters are limited to 40,000 Btu/h, and they may not be the only heat source in a dwelling.

questions.q: The oxygen-depletion safety shutoff on an unvented room heater must shut off gas before oxygen falls below:
questions.why: IFGC 621.6 requires the shutoff set point to be no lower than 18 percent oxygen, and it may not be field adjustable.

questions.q: Without a listed hood or other protection, what vertical clearance does IFGC 623.7 require between a domestic range cooking top and combustible cabinets above?
questions.why: 30 in is required; it may be reduced to 24 in with approved protection such as a metal hood or millboard covered with sheet metal.

questions.q: Unvented infrared radiant heaters totaling 150,000 Btu/h are installed in a shop. Under IFGC 630.3, what is the minimum outdoor ventilation air?
questions.why: The rule is 4 cfm per 1,000 Btu/h of input: 150 x 4 = 600 cfm.

questions.q: A room containing a 100,000 Btu/h furnace is used as the only source of return air. Under IFGC 618.3, the room volume must exceed:
questions.why: The room must have more than 1 cubic foot per 10 Btu/h of total input (100,000 / 10 = 10,000 cubic feet), with return inlets at least 10 ft from any draft hood.

questions.q: Under the 2021 IFGC and IMC, a clothes dryer exhaust terminal must provide an open area of at least:
questions.why: The terminal passageway must be undiminished and provide at least 12.5 square inches of open area.

questions.q: Under 40 CFR 82.161, a technician servicing the AC in a farm tractor cab (an MVAC-like appliance) must hold:
questions.why: MVAC-like appliances (open-drive, 20 lb or less, off-road vehicle cabs) may be serviced by Type II or Section 609 certified technicians.

questions.q: Under 40 CFR 82.152, which activity does NOT count as technician work that requires EPA 608 certification?
c: Attaching gauges to the service ports
questions.why: Work that could break into the refrigerant circuit (hoses, gauges, adding or removing refrigerant, cutting lines) requires certification; painting does not.

questions.q: Under 40 CFR 82.152, a pressure decay test or sight glass check used as a leak inspection must be:
c: Done only by the equipment manufacturer
Paired with a method that locates the leak
questions.why: Those methods only show that a leak exists, so they must be combined with a method that finds where it is, such as a bubble test or electronic detector.

questions.q: Since April 27, 1995, EPA has stayed (not enforced) the refrigerant sales restriction as it applies to:
c: Refrigerant in appliances without fully assembled circuits, such as pre-charged split-system components
questions.why: 82.154(g) stays the sales restriction only for refrigerant contained in appliances without fully assembled refrigerant circuits.

questions.q: Before opening an appliance only to change the compressor oil, 40 CFR 82.156 requires evacuating or pressurizing it to no higher than:
questions.why: For oil changes the appliance (or the receiver the oil is drained into) must be at 5 psig or less.

questions.q: Under 40 CFR 82.156(h), recovered refrigerant may be put back into another appliance without reclaiming it when:
c: The other appliance is owned by the same person
The refrigerant passes a sight-glass check
The other appliance is a motor vehicle AC
questions.why: Refrigerant may go back into the same appliance or another appliance owned by the same person; selling it to another owner requires reclamation.

questions.q: When needed parts are unavailable, how long can EPA's leak repair deadline be extended at most for a system that does not need an industrial process shutdown?
questions.why: The extension runs until 30 days after the part arrives but is capped at 180 days (270 days with an industrial process shutdown).

questions.q: Refrigerant-in-air automatic leak detectors used in place of periodic leak inspections must detect at least ___ and alarm at ___.
questions.why: Direct refrigerant-in-air sensors must accurately detect 10 ppm and alert at 100 ppm.

questions.q: Under the HFC leak repair rule (40 CFR 84.106), which leak rate calculation methods may an owner use?
c: Either annualizing or rolling average, using the same method at all facilities
Any method the technician chooses for each event
questions.why: Owners may use the annualizing or rolling average method but must use the same method at all facilities covered by the rule.

questions.q: Under current 40 CFR 84.54(c)(1), a new residential R-410A (GWP above 700) split system may still be installed when:
c: All of its specified components were made or imported before January 1, 2025
It has a SEER2 rating above 16
questions.why: The rule allows installation where all components were made or imported before January 1, 2025; after the May 2026 amendment there is no installation deadline.

questions.q: Under the AIM Act, what share of the HFC baseline is allowed in 2036 and later?
questions.why: The schedule steps down from 90 to 60 to 30 to 20 percent and reaches 15 percent of baseline (an 85 percent cut) in 2036.

questions.q: A 2,000 sq ft retail sales floor will hold 30 people. Using IMC Table 403.3.1.1 (7.5 cfm per person + 0.12 cfm per sq ft), the breathing-zone outdoor air is:
Under the IMC, automatic controls for an enclosed parking garage ventilation system may never reduce the rate below:
questions.why: The system must be able to deliver 0.75 cfm per sq ft, but automatic operation may not drop below 0.05 cfm per sq ft.

questions.q: Under the 2021 IMC and IRC, external duct insulation and insulated flex duct must be marked with the manufacturer, R-value and fire ratings at intervals of no more than:
questions.why: Both codes require the identification to be printed at intervals not greater than 36 inches.

questions.q: Crimp joints in round metal ducts must be mechanically fastened with at least how many sheet metal screws or rivets, equally spaced?
questions.why: At least three equally spaced screws or rivets are required, with a 1 in minimum lap.

questions.q: Under IMC 2021 607.3.3.1, a fire damper's heat-responsive device must be rated about 50 F above normal duct temperature but not less than:
questions.why: The operating temperature must be about 50 F above the normal duct temperature, but never lower than 160 F.

questions.q: Using IMC Table 1103.1 (R-32 = 4.8 lb per 1,000 cubic feet), about how much R-32 may a single circuit hold if it serves only a 12 x 12 x 8 ft room?
Under IMC 2021 1105.7, pressure relief devices for a refrigeration machinery room must discharge at least how high above adjoining grade?
questions.why: Relief discharge must be at least 15 ft above grade and at least 20 ft from windows, ventilation openings and exits.

questions.q: Refrigerant piping crossing an open passageway, and not run against the ceiling, must be at least how high above the floor under IMC 2021 1107.2?
questions.why: The IMC requires at least 7 ft 3 in of headroom under refrigerant piping crossing a passageway.

questions.q: Under IRC 2021 M2103.4, piping to be embedded in a radiant floor slab must be hydrostatically tested at not less than:
questions.why: The test is at least 100 psi held for 30 minutes while all joints are visually inspected.

questions.q: Using IRC Table M2003.2, what size diaphragm (pressurized) expansion tank is required for a hot water heating system holding 50 gallons?
questions.why: The table lists 4.0 gallons for a diaphragm tank (7.5 gallons nonpressurized) for a 50 gallon system.

questions.q: Under IRC 2021 M2002.4, a boiler relief valve must discharge by gravity to within how many inches of the floor (or to an open receptor)?
questions.why: The discharge must be piped by gravity to within 18 in of the floor or to an open receptor.

questions.q: Under IRC 2021 M1407, an electric duct heater installed within what distance of a heat pump or air conditioner must be listed for that installation?
questions.why: Duct heaters within 4 ft of a heat pump or AC must be listed for that use, and the heat pump or AC must be listed too.

questions.q: While running, a compressor's start (HERM) wire carries 4.0 A and the capacitor reads 380 V. Using uF = 2,652 x A / V, the capacitance is about:
questions.why: 2,652 x 4.0 / 380 = about 27.9 uF, which is then compared to the capacitor's rating.

questions.q: A condensing unit has a 16 A RLA compressor and a 1.2 A fan motor. What is its minimum circuit ampacity?
Under NEC 440.22(A), the branch-circuit protective device for a hermetic compressor normally may not exceed what percent of its rated-load current?
questions.why: The limit is 175 percent, which may be raised to no more than 225 percent if the motor will not start.

questions.q: How do most cylinders for A2L refrigerants such as R-454B differ from A1 refrigerant cylinders?
c: They have left-hand threaded valve outlets and a red band
They have no pressure relief device
They may be refilled with any refrigerant
questions.ref: Arkema Forane tech tip; ACCA HVAC Blog
questions.why: A2L cylinders use left-hand threaded outlets to prevent mix-ups, carry a red band for flammability, and use a reclosing relief valve.

questions.q: With all other appliances off, the 1/2 cubic foot test dial on a natural gas meter makes one revolution in 36 seconds. What is the gas flow?
questions.why: CFH = 3,600 x 0.5 / 36 = 50 CFH, or about 50,000 Btu/h with 1,000 Btu per cubic foot gas.

questions.q: During a decay test after evacuation, the micron reading rises and then levels off well below atmospheric pressure. This most likely means:
c: The system has a large leak
The system is tight but still contains moisture
The vacuum pump oil is fresh
The system is ready to charge
questions.why: A rise that stabilizes indicates moisture still boiling off; a steady rise toward atmospheric indicates a leak.

questions.q: Why must POE oil for R-410A systems be kept in sealed metal containers?
c: It is flammable at room temperature
It absorbs moisture from the air quickly
questions.why: POE absorbs moisture quickly, and water breaks it down into acids that damage the system.

questions.q: DOE's M1 test procedure, used for SEER2 ratings since January 1, 2023, rates ducted systems at an external static pressure of about:
questions.ref: 10 CFR 430 App. M1; NYSERDA fact sheet
questions.why: M1 raised the test external static pressure from about 0.1-0.2 in. w.c. to 0.5 in. w.c., which lowers the ratings.

questions.q: Which ACCA manual covers selecting supply outlets and return grilles to avoid drafts and stagnant air?
questions.why: Manual T (Air Distribution Basics) covers outlet and return selection; J is loads, S is equipment selection and N is commercial loads.

questions.q: Before a Type I grease duct is concealed, IMC 2021 506.3.2.5 requires its welded joints to be checked with:
c: A light test using a lamp of at least 100 watts
A water fill test for 24 hours
questions.why: A lamp of at least 100 watts is passed through the duct to confirm all welded and brazed joints are liquid-tight.

questions.q: Under IRC 2021 M1411.6, refrigerant suction lines must be insulated to at least:
questions.why: Suction line insulation must be at least R-3 with an external surface permeance of 0.05 perm or less.
